podcast.title: RCA Contract and Cautious Approach (1965)
podcast.body: Encouraged by Chet Atkins, a legendary country music producer at RCA, Pride made a demo, leading Atkins to offer him a recording contract in 1965. RCA, however, adopted a cautious approach, initially booking him for shows in different towns to "temperature check" audience reactions before scheduling further performances. "Atkins liked what he heard from Pride and offered him recording contract in 1965."

podcast.title: Addressing His Race in Detroit (1966)
podcast.body: At a show in Detroit in 1966, Pride confronted an audience that greeted him with silence upon realizing he was African American. He introduced himself, acknowledged his "permanent suntan," stated his Mississippi farming background, and declared his intention to entertain them. "friends, I realize it's a little unique me coming out here with a permanent suntan to sing country and western to you. But that's the way it is."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Grand Ole Opry Membership (1967)
podcast.body: In 1967, Charlie Pride became the second African American to be granted membership to the Grand Ole Opry, and the first since harmonica player DeFord Bailey, who last played at the Opry in 1941. This marked a significant milestone for racial integration in country music's premier institution. "Charlie Pride became the second African American ever to be allowed to be a member of the Grand Ole Opera in the first since the harmonica player to Ford Bailey who had last played at the Opera in 1941."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Major Label Exclusivity (1967-1991)
podcast.body: Charlie Pride was the only African-American country singer signed to a major record label, RCA, between 1967 and 1991. This highlights his unique position and the industry's limited diversity during that period. "he was the only African-American country singer that was signed to a major record label between 1967 and 1991. That was RCA."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Television Debut (1967)
podcast.body: Charlie Pride made his television debut in 1967 on "The Lawrence Welk Show," where he performed his breakthrough song, "Just Between You and Me." "In 1967, he made his television debut on the Lawrence Welk show singing just between you and me."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Country Music Association Awards (1971, 1972)
podcast.body: Charlie Pride won the Country Music Association Male Entertainer of the Year award in both 1971 and 1972, marking significant recognition in the country music industry. "He won the Country Music Association Male Entertainer of the Year award in 1971 and 1972."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: View on Country Music Diversity (1973)
podcast.body: In 1973, Charlie Pride articulated a broad perspective on country music, arguing it is "many things" and the "basic music of America," encompassing elements of jazz, blues, and other categories. He believed that various genres were starting to "gel" into "one ball of wax." "Country music is just about time for it to stop being used as a whipping boy. It's good music. It's the basic music of America."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: "You Look Like Them But Sound Like Us"
podcast.body: Charlie Pride was told, "you look like them but sound like us," a comment highlighting his ability to appeal across racial lines in the country music genre. "Pride was told you look like them but sound like us."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Career Focus on Country
podcast.body: Despite the pop crossover success of "Kiss an Angel Good Morning," Charlie Pride's other hits primarily charted on the country charts. He was content with this, viewing himself primarily as a country artist not seeking a pop career. "His other hits were on the country charts, which I think he was just fine with because he was a country artist who was not looking for a pop career."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Comparison to Linda Martell
podcast.body: Charlie Pride was frequently used as the frame of reference for any African American country singer, including Linda Martell, who was often referred to as "the female Charlie Pride." Unlike Martell, displaying his face on album covers eventually became a non-issue, and he made numerous television appearances. "Linda fits the pride pattern. Typical, as she was frequently referred to as the female Charlie Pride."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Discovery in Montana
podcast.body: Pride was discovered singing in country clubs in Montana, a state that had the fewest black people in the union at the time. He had lived there for a decade before being encouraged to record a demo. "He was discovered when he was singing in country clubs in Montana of all places."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Early Life and Baseball Career
podcast.body: Born into poverty in Mississippi, Charlie Pride initially pursued a career in baseball, playing in the Negro leagues. He was paid extra to sing before games to boost attendance, but his baseball career was cut short by an elbow injury. "he did play in the Negro leagues and he was paid extra to sing before games to encourage attendance, but that career, the baseball career, was derailed by an elbow injury."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Example of Non-Black Soulfulness
podcast.body: Tom Bell cited Charlie Pride, a straightforward country singer, as a prime example to underscore his conviction that "soulful" qualities in music are not exclusively inherent to Black artists. "Look at Charlie Pride, he's a straight country singer."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Experience with Racism (Personal Account)
podcast.body: Charlie Pride stated that he never experienced anyone yelling a slur at him or telling him to leave the stage. He attributed this to his belief in his identity as "Charlie Pride, the American singing musician," suggesting people might accept you as you believe yourself to be. "Pride said that there was never a time when anyone yelled to slur at him and shouted at him and told him to get off the stage."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Extensive Chart Success
podcast.body: Between 1969 and 1983, Charlie Pride recorded an impressive 24 number one country songs, establishing him as one of country music's most successful artists. "He went on to record 24 number one country songs between 1969 and 1983."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Initial Obscuring of Race by RCA
podcast.body: Early in his career, RCA avoided using Charlie Pride's photo on promotional materials. While his voice created demand, many listeners were unaware he was African American. "up to this point, RCA was not using Pride's photo on anything."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Nashville" Character
podcast.body: The character of Tommy Brown in Robert Altman's 1975 film "Nashville" was widely believed to be based on Charlie Pride due to the actor's resemblance in hairstyle and dress, and Pride's unique status as a prominent black country singer. Pride, however, denied any connection, stating that if it was meant to be him, it was "a lie." "The film director, Robert Altman, made a movie about the country music industry which came out in 1975 and he included a character that many people believed was supposed to be Charlie Pride."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Manager Jack Clement
podcast.body: Charlie Pride's manager was Jack Clement, known for his unconventional and innovative approach in the music industry. "His manager was Jack Clement, who was known for thinking outside the box."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Touring Demands
podcast.body: Pride faced extensive touring demands early in his career, often spending long periods away from home. He once recounted being away for three months straight, longer than his military service. "I was away from home one time for three months and never got back home."
